Mrs. S is an attractive, athletically built mother in her late thirties.1 She had originally begun psychotherapy in another city when she had been in a state of severe anxiety and distress. Commentary

Robert Michels MD

Robert Michels

525 East 68th Street
New York, NY 10021

Robert Michels  

The title of the conference, “The Intrapsychic and Interpersonal Dimensions: An Unresolved Dilemma,” leads me to observe that, in fact, true intellectual dilemmas are never resolved; they just fade away, replaced by new and more interesting dilemmas. We have seen that this earlier dilemma no longer has much heat attached to it, although there are still residual loyalties to the leaders who bore the banners in the former disputes. More important, a series of new dilemmas have moved to center stage and now occupy our attention.

One theme of the panel offers an illustration. Mitchell, in his brilliant summary of the historical background of the dilemma, warns us to be careful not to read too casually. He points out two important things about Sullivan's interpersonal model. First, that Sullivan was fighting not with Freud but rather with Kraepelin. The “interpersonal” paradigm was designed as an antidote to the brain-constitutional diathesis that was the popular alternative. Second, that Sullivan did modify one element of Freud. In shifting from the centrality of an “inner drive program” of psychic development to an “environmental experience and secondary internalization” model of psychic development, Sullivan was bothered by Freud's preoccupation with the drive origin of mental life and modified this aspect of Freud's theory in his psychology.

Dr. Michels is Barklie McKee Henry Professor and Chairman, Department of Psychiatry, Cornell University Medical College; Psychiatrist-in-Chief, The New York Hospital; and Supervising and Training Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

Epilogue

Donald Silver Issue Editor

Donald Silver

Donald Silver  

James Joyce wrote to Nora, his fiance, “O that I could nestle in your womb like a child born of your flesh and blood, be fed by your blood, sleep in the warm secret gloom of your body!” after the death of his mother, when his loneliness was at a peak. To Joyce, who witnessed 11 of his mother's pregnancies, the physical development of the fetus in the womb, and development of the child in the family, parallel the soul's development, or what we call self development. Just as the fetus develops in the womb and the infant within the family, the soul, or self, develops within the mind of each man. Thus for Joyce this concept of pregnancy was the model of the epigenesis of the soul that became the basis of his creative work as he traced his own soul's development in his autobiographic novels.

Despite its rich potential, the topic of pregnancy has been largely neglected in psychoanalytic writings. We hope that the preceding essays will mitigate this neglect and that the essays will stimulate further research and elaboration. The study of pregnancy offers us the opportunity to understand the earliest development of object relations, of confronting the instinctual conflicts associated with the creation of new life, and of observing the dynamic interplay of psyche and soma in problems of conception, gestation, and delivery. By understanding the psychological meaning of pregnancy, we can begin to understand, in greater detail than ever before, the fantasies associated with the creation as well as the destruction of life.

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Two decades have passed since Otto Kernberg began publishing his views on borderline patients. He believes they comprise a distinct diagnostic group based on a special type of ego structure and object relations. His use of formulations from the object relation theorists, Melanie Klein, Edith Jacobson, and Margaret Mahler, demonstrated to many in the analytic community the value of a greater familiarity with their formulations and the importance of assimilating these formulations into classical psychoanalysis.

The response to Kernberg's writing was enormously enthusiastic. A flurry of papers, symposia and conferences on the borderline concept followed, and the consideration of treating the severely disturbed patient with analytic methods increased.

Six years ago Abend, Porder, and Willick published Borderline Patients: Psychoanalytic Perspectives, a book based on the proceedings of the Kris Study Group of the New York Psychoanalytic Institute from 1973 to 1977 and an extended meeting with Otto Kernberg. The analyses of four patients who were considered borderline were used as the clinical data for the authors' conclusions.

The conclusions were in disagreement with the views of Kernberg and others on borderline patients. Abend, Porder, and Willick stated that many conceptualizations pertaining to borderline patients were phenomenological descriptions or abstract generalities that could not be confirmed in their data.

Bewilderment and the Borderline Phenomenon

Peter Giovacchini MD

Peter Giovacchini

270 Locust Road
Winnetka, IL 60093

Peter Giovacchini  

During the past decade, psychoanalysis as a therapeutic system has been increasingly challenged. Some clinicians believe that “psychoanalysis is dead,” a pronouncement that has sometimes been made by psychoanalysts. Others strongly feel that psychoanalysis, as a separate organized discipline, will not last much longer.

Undoubtedly, there are many complex reasons for such gloomy predictions. Unlike the opposition that psychoanalysis initially encountered, there is relatively little objection to it as a conceptual system. Overtly or covertly, as a method of understanding, it has had a significant influence on both the arts and sciences. Its efficacy as a therapeutic procedure, however, has been severely attacked.

As practitioners, we believe the essence of psychoanalysis resides in its clinical explanations and the study of the treatment process. Initially it was prescribed for a small group of patients, those that Freud (1914) called the transference neuroses. I recall how my peer group, as young clinicians, eagerly sought the analyzable patient, since the patients we commonly encountered could not be fit into the diagnostic category of transference neurosis.

Dr. Giovacchini is Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, University of Illinois College of Medicine and Director, Center for Psychoanalytic Studies, Chicago, Illinois.

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Although the papers reflect a diversity of opinion, the contributors are all unanimous regarding the importance of the detailed analytic investigation of the borderline patient by Abend, Porder, and Willick.

The differences in opinion can be organized around two issues: (1) the concept of deficit in psychoanalysis; (2) the concepts that have the most explanatory value in the psychoanalysis of the borderline patient. Abend, Porder, Willick, Weinshel, and Wurmser agree on the importance of deficit in the borderline patient but they believe deficit can exist only as part of the complexity of psychic conflict that embodies wish, defense, and compromise formation. Adler, Grotstein, Giovacchini, and Meissner understand deficit existing outside of conflict and thus requiring a therapeutic technique different from that employed with conflict.

Several contributors — Grotstein, Giovacchini, and Adler — agree that the concepts of classical analysis are inadequate to explain the special interaction and transference of the borderline patient.

From the papers we see a tempering of the polarity of opinion and the hold on psychoanalysis of some of Kernberg's initial formulations on the borderline patient. Further modification and assimilation of the diversity of views can occur only with the type of investigation that has been presented by Abend, Porder, and Willick.

Prologue

L. Levi MD and David Scharff Issue Co-Editors

David Scharff

David Scharff  

These papers and the discussions of them were prepared for a conference on “The Intrapsychic and Interpersonal Dimensions: An Unresolved Dilemma,” held in April 1987 to honor the fiftieth anniversary of the Washington School of Psychiatry. Harry Stack Sullivan, a most active participant in the early years of the school, challenged the intrapsychic focus of Freud's theories with his interpersonal perspective, with resulting alternative theories and therapeutic approaches. Conference participants sought to trace how these differences in psychoanalytic theory and practice have been elaborated or resolved in the years since their initial assertion.

In the first of the conference's three sections, Drs. John Gedo and Stephen Mitchell presented the historical perspective, while Drs. Sander Abend and Daniel Stern focussed on theoretical issues. Dr. Earl Wittenberg then offered some informal comments. Next, material from an analytic case was presented, a case chosen for its typicality and because the analyst had been trained in the classical tradition. This material was discussed by Drs. Herbert Schlesinger, Paulina Kernberg, and Ernest Wolf; they seem to articulate respectively intrapsychic, object relations, and self psychology points of view on the therapeutic process. Dr. Edgar Levenson, usually regarded as an interpersonalist, prepared his critique from both theoretical and clinical perspectives. Finally, Drs. Arnold Cooper, Robert Michels, and Joseph Lichtenberg were asked to discuss whether we can solve the dilemma, based on responses to the papers and the case discussion.

Case Discussion and Position Statement

Paulina Kernberg MD

Paulina Kernberg

21 Bloomingdale Road
White Plains, NY 10605n

Paulina Kernberg  

Any separation of the intrapsychic from the interactional or interpersonal is arbitrary. Those who think that the patient is replicating, in the present, interactional patterns of his childhood of the past, neglect the fact that these patterns are transformed and structuralized intrapsychically. There is no simple blind repetition of the past in the present. The past is organized within the subjectivity of the individual into structures. It is this internalized structure which is replayed. Escalona (1968) used the phrase “pattern of concrete experience” to delineate an intermediate domain where individual endowment and stimuli from the environment blend in subjective experience, which in turn affects and influences further interactions with the environment. Thus, the intrapsychic and the interpersonal are in ongoing interchange through projection or introjection, or, in other terms, through assimilation or accommodation.

The more severe the psychopathology, the wider the gap between actual and intrapsychic experience, and the less direct is the relation between present and past experience, as well as the influence of the past on the present.

Dr. Kernberg is Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Cornell University Medical College; Director, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, The New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center, Westchester Division; and Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

The word borderline has been a particularly conspicuous one in the psychoanalytic lexicon during the last quarter of a century. It has also been a most troublesome word, one that means many different things to so many of us. The fact that it has become a modifier for so many nouns — borderline patients, borderline conditions, borderline states, borderline disorders, borderline organization, borderline personality, as well as borderline group of neuroses — is already an ominous indication of its diverse and idiosyncratic meanings, some of which are mere nuances but some of which presage differences that can be light years apart. The embarrassing fact that, as a discipline, we are not even sure what the word really means to all of us, is sufficient reason for our considerable discontent.

Commentary

Arnold Cooper MD

Arnold Cooper

525 East 68th Street
New York, NY 10021

Arnold Cooper  

The question “what is psychoanalysis?” has emerged as a central theme of this conference, and, of course, attempts to probe this question raise important issues of theoretical strategy. Gedo and several other participants see psychoanalysis as a very broad enterprise, encompassing a large variety of ideas and techniques, including many of an educational and suggestive nature. Technical interventions that many analysts would label “not analytic” fall comfortably within Gedo's concept of psychoanalysis. On the other hand, psychoanalysts interested in sharpening the distinction between psychoanalysis and psychotherapy suggest that “you may be carrying out a variety of measures that help your patient, but your procedure should not be labeled psychoanalysis.” Abend, I believe, has taken that stance, agreeing that Gedo's view of treatment is interesting and helpful, but not all of it can be included under the heading of psychoanalysis. Innovations in psychoanalytic theory and technique have always been sharply challenged, and it is a traditional concern that psychoanalysis not become contaminated with other therapeutic modes.

I would like to suggest that the definition of psychoanalysis be held open and that our boundaries remain fuzzy. Rather than making a definitive decision about what psychoanalysis is and, therefore, what the area of our study is, I would prefer that we continually arrive at new definitions of psychoanalysis, modifying each as we increase our knowledge of intrapsychic and interpersonal aspects of human behavior.

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 Eighteenth Street N.W.
Washington, DC 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

The conference leads me to conclude that intrapsychic and interpersonal no longer serve as banners under which opposing camps of Freudian traditionalists and Sullivanian revisionists rally followers. The duality between intrapsychic and interpersonal has been restated in a multiplicity of different forms, but the broad divergence of these two conceptual positions is never fully resolved. I conclude also that as each of the current forms given to this problem is laid out before us by the presenters, the lack of suitable data has been cited recurrently as a source of difficulty in working toward a resolution.

Gedo redefines the problem by placing character as the bridging concept between the intrapsychic and interpersonal realms of discourse. Character pathology refers simultaneously to maladaptive psychological structures (intrapsychic) and to overt behaviors produced by their activation, that is, by the individual's transactions with the environment (interpersonal). Enactments based on character interface the two realms. Gedo notes the polarization between theories that emphasize later (oedipal and postoedipal) development and those that emphasize early (preoedipal dyadic) development. Parallel is the polarization centering on the degree of influence of environmental input. Gedo warns that interpersonal transactions, enactments, and even well-observed transferences are at best an imperfect window to the historic intrapsychic developments; reading backward to specific stages is often a genetic fallacy.

578

Failure of Psychological Gestation

Donald Silver MD and B. Campbell PHD

B. Campbell

26111 Fourteen Mile Road, #103
Franklin, MI 48025

B. Campbell  

Certain physical events throughout the life cycle alter us in unique ways, after which we are not and cannot be the same as we were before. Such important events in a woman's life include menarche, pregnancy, and menopause. Accompanying each are psychological changes in self-image, the sense of identity, and self-esteem. We are well acquainted with the psychology of the anorexic adolescent who denies her potential for motherhood (Wilson, 1985) and with that of the menopausal woman whose potential for motherhood is lost (Deutsch, 1945; Benedek, 1950). We are not so well acquainted with the psychology of the pregnant woman.

Freud (1904, 1913, 1915, 1937) suggested that psychoanalysis should be postponed when a person may be preoccupied by a crisis, an illness, or during physiological periods of dramatic change. He noted that when the ego's whole interest is taken up by reality it withholds itself from the analytic work. Helena Deutsch was impressed by Freud's ideas long before she moved to Vienna in 1918 to begin her analysis with him. She then became a devoted analysand and a friend as well as a dedicated student (Roazen, 1985). We think it safe to assume that, insofar as Deutsch had suffered several miscarriages prior to her analysis, pregnancy was subject to some discussion if not exploration.

Dr. Silver is an Assistant Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Wayne State University College of Medicine; he is also a Lecturer at the Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.

Prologue

Eloise Agger D.S.W.

Eloise Agger

Eloise Agger  

Keeping in mind the credo of this journal that understanding of clinical phenomena is enhanced by viewing them from the multiple metapsychological perspectives of structural theory, object relations development, and self psychology, it seems timely to now address the nature of sibling relationships. The topic is deceptive in its everyday familiarity. We take its history for granted. However, our patients tell us repeatedly in their many languages that what may seem familiar is not at all obvious. To inattend is to inadvertently reinforce contempt for sibling objects and, further, to profane those early relationships that may have served to keep the other relationships, between parents and child, as it were, sacred. Freud addressed this possibility as early as 1897 in writing about endopsychic myths that may grow out of conflict in the nursery and be reflected throughout life within intrapsychic structures that govern our affective, cognitive and object investments.

Charting the course of sibling relationships from childhood into adulthood from several psychoanalytic perspectives may contribute to a much needed metapsychological assessment of sibling influence on early formations of the ego, sense of self, drive regulation, narcissistic advances, and development of object relations. Equally important is increased awareness of the transformations that take place over the span of time as maturation and oedipal effects are factored into mental equations.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Eloise Agger D.S.W. Issue Editor

Eloise Agger

Eloise Agger  

Each of the contributors to this issue has observed sibling relationships to be significant in new and unexpected ways. Parens discovered the sibling potential as a bridging object. Kernberg and Richards speak of the sibling function which lead to the development of a sense of “we-ness.” Balsam sorts out the separate lines of parental and sibling transference which reveal aspects of the ego ideal. Graham establishes a model for analyzing the intricate evolution of the sibling transference. Wilson illustrates how the threads of psychic reality and autobiography can be blended to energize and enrich the creative process and product.

Perhaps much that is joyful and ambitious in our object love and in narcissistically gratifying adult achievements can be traced back to our early relationships with our siblings, whether real or imagined, alive, or dead. To the extent that we can acknowledge and work through the Schadenfreude — taking malicious pleasure in someone else's misfortune — that characterizes those relationships, we may experience the full affective force of the preoedipal parricidal, incestuous inclinations that tie us to our particular genetic configurations. From there, it may well take many more years of analytic work and conceptual formulation to arrive at the point of reconciliation where murderous feelings, derivatives of the aggressive drive, are recognized as natural responses to grave narcissistic assault. Resolution of the conflict and inhibitions that surround these feelings and pose obstacles to healthy selfobject development precedes the capacity to love, invest, value, lose, despair, and differentiate intrapsychically. Only then may we expect to realistically atone, make restitution in a symbolic sense, and to become one with our completed self.

Childbearing and Child Rearing

Kerry Novick

Kerry Novick

617 Stratford
Ann Arbor, MI 48104

Kerry Novick  

Childbearing, which includes pregnancy, birth, and the early nursing period, and child rearing — that is, the bringing up and taking care of children — are often differently perceived in our society, and by women themselves.1 Pregnant and nursing mothers experience enhanced narcissism, describe themselves as precious, and occupy an almost mystical position in the cultural perception of our society, now and in the past, vide the power of the image of the Madonna and Child. But has anyone ever seen a picture of Mary toilet-training Jesus? Something seems to change in our perception and valuation of the mother-child relationship by the end of the first year; many women doubt the worth of child rearing, and our society seems unsure of the social role and importance of bringing up children. Why should this be so? I would like to explore some of the childhood roots of these attitudes in women and suggest that childbearing and child rearing constitute separate strands in feminine development, strands that may come together only at the close of adolescence.

The time around 18 months seems crucial in many areas of a little girl's development. Firstly, she is consolidating a self-other distinction which is rooted in her relationship with her primary object, usually the mother.

Kerry Kelly Novick is member of the Faculty, Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.

Adolescent Pregnancy and Motherhood: A Psychoanalytical Perspective

Dinora Pines MD

Dinora Pines

16 Bracknell Gardens
London NW3 7EB, England

Dinora Pines  

It is striking that despite advances in contraception and the easy availability of termination of pregnancy a considerable number of teenage girls still become pregnant, and some become teenage mothers. For many of them the normal developmental crises of puberty and adolescence, followed by that of first pregnancy and motherhood, facilitate further psychic growth. For others these crises may revive primitive anxieties and conflicts belonging to previous developmental phases, which cause them to regress. For some of these young mothers the birth of a real baby may prove to be a calamity. The physical maturity of puberty offers them an alternative means of resolving psychic conflict and establishing their femininity. While a girl's wish to be pregnant may be seen as part of normal adolescent development, a further step in maturation evokes a wish to bring a live child into the world and achieve fulfillment of the maternal ego-ideal. The adolescent girls I am discussing, however, appear to have taken only the first part of this developmental step. In this paper I focus on the unconscious conflicts of some immature young women that prevent them from establishing good-enough mothering (Winnicott, 1960).

Dr. Pines is a Training and Supervising Analyst, British Institute of Psychoanalysis.

Having reviewed the psychoanalytic literature pertaining to femininity, the reproductive urge in women, and the preparation for pregnancy and motherhood, we now offer clinical material from three pregnant women, one of whom had two consecutive pregnancies while still in analysis. As already noted, Freud's proposition that the wish for pregnancy and for the baby as reparative has been seriously challenged. Subsequent investigators conclude that the wish for pregnancy and motherhood represents a fundamental psychobiological expression of femininity and relates biologically to the maturation of the reproductive organs and psychologically to an identification with mother.

Bibring was the first analyst to focus specifically on pregnancy as a crucial phase in the female life cycle. She and her co-workers (1961) proposed the concept of pregnancy as a maturational crisis. This work, however, although conceived within an analytic frame of reference was based primarily on periodic interviews of a number of primiparae during pregnancy and during the postnatal period.

Henri Parens MD

Henri Parens

3200 Henry Avenue
Philadelphia, PA 19129

Henri Parens  

Athough the importance of siblings is well appreciated in clinical psychoanalysis, what we analysts know of the subject, to the best of my knowledge, has not to date been topically conceptualized and organized. Most of our attention in discussing genetics and dynamics of intrapsychic conflicts, objects relations, and the development of object relatedness has been given to the parent-child relationships. Furthermore, psychoanalysts generally agree that in the clinical situation representations of the parents are the central objects in the transference, and representations of siblings are not usually externalized onto the analyst to become central transference objects.

Nonetheless, in both adult and child clinical analytic work, our patients' siblings become known to us to a greater or lesser extent. In fact in some patients, siblings play a vital part in the analysis of their neurotic conflicts and symptoms. To the extent that they are selected objects vital to our patients' neurosis-inducing fantasies, episodic sibling transference constellations do occur. In one instance, my patient's transference allowed the analysis not only of her brother's seducing her but, critical to her neurosis, of the part she played in that seduction as well as her reactions to it and to him.

Henri Parens is Training and Supervising Analyst, Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute; Research Professor in Psychiatry and Director of the Infant Psychiatry Section, The Medical College of Pennsylvania.

Relatively little has been written about the pregnancy of the psychoanalyst, and the papers that have been written have been limited essentially to case reports from individual practices (Hannett, 1949; van Leeuwen, 1966; Lax, 1969; Braasch, 1979). In contrast, the small but substantial literature on the psychotherapist's pregnancy (Nadelson et al., 1974; Clarkson, 1980; Penn, 1986) includes a book based on a prospective study involving interviews with therapists during and after their first pregnancies (Fenster et al., 1986). In order to redress the balance and learn more about the impact of the analyst's pregnancy on the course of analysis I conducted a retrospective study based on interviews with 12 analysts and my own experience as a pregnant analyst.

Methods

I requested interviews with 18 women who had completed one or more pregnancies while practicing analysis. All were candidates at or graduates of accredited training institutes of the American Psychoanalytic Association. Six women declined to be interviewed.

Until fairly recently, theoretical and clinical distinctions in psychoanalysis were hard-edged and uncompromising. This conference represents a noteworthy ecumenical effort, an attempt to arrive at some consensus among divergent groups. Unfortunately, ecumenicism, however much to be desired, entails its own liabilities. First, there is a certain confusion of tongues. Psychoanalysts use language which is highly loaded with implied meanings. Much as “the Flag” carries powerful emotional and contextual values, “resistance,” “transference,” “drive” are all terms that accrue their meaning from a particular theoretical stance and, moreover, may have a different meaning and set of referents for someone holding another metapsychological position.

Not only is there a confusion of semantics, but different analysts are, figuratively speaking, seeing different patients; that is, the same patient will look different from different perspectives. This “preconfiguration” as Heidegger called it, was strikingly evident in the response of the panel to the clinical material presented. Rather than arriving at different formulations based on the material presented, each wanted new information, in essence, another view of the patient.

Ever since Freud first articulated his theories of female sexual development (1905, 1924, 1931, 1933) there have been some sharp differences of opinion on the subject among analysts as well as nonanalysts. Various aspects of these differences have been discussed and debated over the years (Horney, 1924, 1926, 1933; Deutsch, 1930, 1945; Jones, 1927, 1935; see Fliegel, 1982 and Chehrazi, 1986 for reviews), but less explicit emphasis has been placed on the question of the origin of the wish for a child in girls.

It is inevitable that one's attention should currently be drawn to the issue because of the striking pressure to have children which has become manifest in women in their thirties who have deferred childbearing or who even had doubted whether they ever wanted to have children. Such pressure would not have been observable readily and so commonly in former times when either absent or imperfect birth control methods did not permit such decisions; or women had no reason for deferring having children since other careers were not widely open to them.

Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Sibling Relationships

Eloise Agger D.S.W.

Eloise Agger

Suite 227 West
7315 Wisconsin Avenue
Bethesda, MD 20814

Eloise Agger  

Much has been written about the significance of parental figures in early human development. Interactions with the primary maternal object are thought to determine the child's progress along the separation-individuation continuum, the establishment of object constancy, and the emergence of a coherent sense of self. The mother-child dyad does not, however, exist within a void; fathers and siblings represent significant variables which affect maternal attitudes and behavior on both conscious and unconscious levels. Infant/child observation research tells us that the child's sensory perceptions of siblings can occur almost as early and with as much frequency as those of the maternal object. While the mother is usually the first love object and the immediate source for identification and early learning, the existence of actual siblings as well as internal sibling representations within the mother's psyche exert a sizeable effect upon the child's ego development. This may occur even before the father's presence is recognized as an accountable force.

In addition to preexisting siblings who form the context into which a child is born and will adapt, the subsequent births of siblings threaten family equilibrium and require further ongoing assessment and adaptation by the individual ego.

Dr. Agger is a member of the Adjunct Clinical Faculty, Catholic University School of Social Work.

Rosemary Balsam M.R.C.P. (Edin.) M.R.C. Psych. (Lond.)

63 Trumbull Street

Rosemary Balsam  

Many an adolescent analysand, at some moment in the analytic journey, considers himself or herself “a good person.” The self-evaluation at that moment will mesh with fantasies of how he or she is perceived by the analyst. When this state is achieved, a unique sense of self-satisfaction and peace permeates the atmosphere. The wish can often be identified as part of childhood experience. I hope to show that in such instances an overt or implied comparison with a sibling can be involved; I wish to consider here only the relation of subjective states of goodness to internalized representations of sibling interaction.

The articulated state of being good, with its outward presumption of shared approved value, is subject to the inner influence of self and object representations as they meld with the hierarchical layers of psychosexual development, their drive derivatives, and the contemporary reverberation with the analytic environment. The meanings of a personal state of goodness within the analytic experience are often illuminated in contrast to the patients' sense of badness.

Arlene Richards  

The presence of siblings as a source of pathology first came to the attention of analysts in terms of sibling rivalry (Levy, 1939). Pfister (1924) had emphasized the love of children for their parents and the readiness with which this love is displaced onto brothers and sisters. He believed that the intensity of the sibling relationship is greater when the relationship to the parents is disturbed or inadequate, that siblings are used to supplement what is missing in the parent-child interaction. The complexity of the relationship to siblings, which calls forth ego functions of observation and integration, is illustrated in his assertion that sibling love invariably covers over unconscious envy, jealousy, a checked lust for power, malicious delight, and frustrated love. Similarly, surface anger may mask suppressed or repressed loving feelings. In this way unconscious rage toward siblings is paradigmatic of what goes wrong with sibling relationships. With this contact between love and rivalrous hatred as a background, it is interesting to reread Freud's major cases to see what data he noted on siblings and what use he made of those data.

In the discussions about and the treatment of psychopathology and psychodynamics there has been in the past three decades a shift toward increasing stress on the similarities with the psychoses and emphasizing the archaic nature of the inner processes. With that there has come a special regard both for the diagnosis of “borderline pathology” with a radically altered understanding and approach toward the severer forms of psychopathology and an increasing reliance on “defect psychology.” This change has had great implications for the attitude toward patients and, more specifically, the treatment approach and poses many questions of validity of claims, of coherence with other lines of research, and of clinical, long-range effectiveness.

Abend, Porder, and Willick have made a courageous attempt to explore these claims, one by one, to stem the tide of clinical revisionism and return to a “classical” method of defense analysis and conflict resolution. “In our view, the major principle of technique with borderlines is the need to maintain, insofar as possible, an analytic relationship with the patient … and not to substitute for it an exhortatory, educational, or managerial one” (p. 202).

Pregnancy: Theoretical Considerations

Malkah Notman MD and Eva Lester MD

Eva Lester

1493 Cambridge Street
Cambridge, MA 02139

Eva Lester  

For a woman, knowing that she is capable of bearing children has been critical in the development of her sense of femininity, gender identity, and self-esteem, even if as an adult she chooses not to actually have children. The awareness of her reproductive potential is part of her self-image.

The social changes of the past two decades have brought with them shifts in family patterns and lifestyles. With more effective control of contraception possible, and many more women working, women have been seeking fulfillment in terms other than a career of motherhood. Having a baby, although a pivotal event psychologically and physically, may not provide the only path to attain status as an adult woman. The implications of these changes for the development of those women who do not have children are now being explored by those concerned with adult development.

Many women have been delaying pregnancy, thus becoming mothers at a time when individuation, ego development, and consolidation of self have progressed to a level different from that of a younger women. This trend raises questions about the effects of the life stage of the individual on the significance and course of the pregnancy.

Malkah T. Notman, M.D. is Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Tufts University Medical School, Boston.

Freud's revision of psychoanalytic theory in the 1920's—the change from the topographic model enunciated in “The Interpretation of Dreams” (1900) to the structural one of “The Ego and the Id” (1923) and from motivational postulates based entirely on instinctual drives to the acknowledgment of the power of the compulsion to repeat—led to a corresponding shift of the focus of psychoanalytic attention from exclusive study of processes in the psychological depths to that of adaptation in the broader sense (see Hartmann, 1939). The concept bridging these two realms of discourse was that of character (cf. Reich, 1930). In the psychoanalytic sense, this is understood as a set of structured mental dispositions that mediate the individual's transactions with his environment, most particularly with the world of his living objects. Hence, character pathology straddles the dividing line between the intrapsychic frame of reference and that of interpersonal relationships: it refers simultaneously to maladaptive psychological structures and to the overt behaviors produced by their activation.

It is frequently true that such a choice of alternative viewpoints leads to seemingly irreconcilable differences among groups of psychoanalysts (see Gedo, 1986).

Dr. Gedo is a Training and Supervisory Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis; he is the author, most recently, of The Mind in Disorder (1988, The Analytic Press), where an earlier version of this material was published.

Daniel Stern  

I will talk from the point of view of the developmental aspects of this problem. I am grateful to Stephen Mitchell for introducing some of the important distinctions between what we call intrapsychic and interpersonal, between fantasy and perception, between psychic reality and actuality, and between inner and outer worlds. The position that I take as a developmentalist is different from that taken by Abend, who posed the confrontation between interpersonal and intrapsychic as a dilemma. If we have to call it a dilemma, it seems to me that it is the right dilemma. Or rather, it is precisely the dialogue or dialectic that is crucial for understanding development. In fact, no other dialectic is of any interest from the clinical point of view of development than the difference and interaction between the intrapsychic and the interpersonal as broadly defined; this is especially so in conceptualizing how it is possible for us to create a world of representations.

We are not talking about the dialectic between nature and nurture. We all agree that the subjective world is a mental construction that emerges from the interaction between “actuality” and the mental processes that encounter that actuality and fashion it into a subjective psychic reality.

I am relieved to have been asked to discuss the relationship between the “intrapsychic” and the “interpersonal” from a Sullivanian perspective, rather than the Sullivanian perspective, since Sullivan's work lends itself to many different readings, and various contemporary writers of often dramatically different points of view all identify themselves as interpersonalists and/or Sullivanians. Prologue

B. Campbell Issue Editor

B. Campbell

B. Campbell  

This issue of psychoanalytic inquiry brings together nine papers filled with clinical and theoretical data which we hope will enrich the psychoanalytic literature on the topic of pregnancy. These papers represent a timely contribution because today's woman is able to choose whether or not she will become pregnant, see her pregnancy to term, and nurture her child.

Pregnancy is a time of change, a time when women can begin to understand themselves as they are, as they were, and as they are becoming. This process of review and recapitulation parallels the physiological changes of pregnancy and has been termed psychological gestation by two of the co-editors of this issue. In our paper we offer the thesis that when there is a failure of psychological gestation, the mother and the infant are at risk for disturbances of attachment.

A theme central to all the papers contained here is that the experience of pregnancy is laden with the burden of the past. In case after case, pregenital issues especially appear to be reworked and resolved during the gestation period. What is remarkable is the consistency with which analysts across nations recognized the important role of the early mother-daughter/father-daughter relationships in negotiating the tasks of pregnancy, the “psychological gestation” that must be completed to allow mother-infant attachment to proceed.

We are fortunate to be able to publish two contributions by Malkah Notman and Eva Lester, both of whom have had an enduring interest in the topic of pregnancy and parenthood.

Alan Gurwitt MD

Alan Gurwitt

61 South Main Street

Alan Gurwitt  

This paper focuses on some of the recently gained understanding of psychological events within expectant fathers and the implications for their wives and children-to-be. After an introduction that addresses the significant changes in attitude toward fathers and expectant fathers, I review some of our new understandings of the roles of fathers and the literature on pathological reactions in men to pregnancy; I then take a look at the evolution of paternal identity and review present understanding of the psychological currents in expectant fathers and the family reverberations.

Introduction

Overt interest in pregnancy has essentially been the domain of women. This is so partly for obvious biological reasons, but clearly social custom and psychological factors have also played a part. Tucker (1974) tells us that it was not until the middle of the 16th century that men made their way into the delivery room. Until then there were severe penalities for any male who attempted to view a birth. Perhaps the most celebrated example is that of Dr. Wertt of Hamburg.

In her chapter on pregnancy, Helene Deutsch (1945) wrote (p. 161): “If it were possible, as in a laboratory, to isolate the phenomenon of pregnancy from all the influences of past and present environment, and to observe directly all the stirrings of the soul that go hand in hand with the development of the fetus, we should probably learn much more about the subtle correlations between mother and fetus.” But psychoanalysis is not a laboratory, and women do not enter it solely to examine the psychological processes of pregnancy. Even if they did, it is likely that, as Deutsch says of her analysands, their fantasies and dreams would be influenced more by the analytic situation and the analyst's attitude than by the fact of pregnancy. Deutsch goes on, however, to express “ … the distinct and very curious impression that the various ontogenetic phases of the fetus affected the psychoanalytic material, especially the dream life of the pregnant woman.”

The account that follows is of a brief psychoanalysis that demonstrates some of the “subtle correlations between mother and fetus” that Deutsch suggests.

A Critique of Borderline Patients: Psychoanalytic Perspectives

James Grotstein MD

James Grotstein

522 Dalehurst Avenue

James Grotstein  

This monograph of the Kris Study group of New York represents a noteworthy, diligent, and candid effort by classical psychoanalysts of the American School, obviously steeped in the perspective of ego psychology and the hegemony of the Oedipus complex, to come to grips with the challenges to American classical theory imposed by the borderline entity. The interest in the borderline disorder came about in no small measure from the Menninger Psychotherapy Research Project (Kernberg et al., 1972), summarized by Wallerstein (1986). Interest has also been propelled by the influence of Kleinian and British Object Relations analysts as well as those in other parts of the world whose views of analysis were informed by psychoanalytic paradigms which allowed them to tread with confidence into the earlier recesses of infant development and, consequently, to be able meaningfully to decipher experiences in the vast array of primitive emotional feelings, thinking, and behavior as they present themselves in the consulting room and hospital.

Dr. Grotstein is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at UCLA; Training and supervising Analyst at the Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Institute, Attending Staff Physician at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center; and Director of the Interdisciplinary Group for Advanced Studies in Primitive Mental States.

Epilogue: Countertransference as the Interface Between the Intrapsychic and the Interpersonal

David Scharff MD

David Scharff

1610 New Hampshire Ave. NW
Washington, DC 20009

David Scharff  

The preceding papers suggest that the debate on the interpersonal versus the intrapsychic points of view be moved to a new level — one of synthesis. There seems to be a consensus among the contributors that the old conflict is no longer a major focus for debate, demonstrating that developments in psychoanalysis over the last 40 years have already been influenced by the interpersonal perspective. No one any longer sees the individual as unfolding sui generis. But an interesting new current has arisen in the last 20 years. The findings of infant and child observational research now enable us to describe inherent characteristics of the infant — indeed of the fetus — which, if they do not confirm the existence of Freud's drives, nevertheless testify to the existence of biological structures that are not very distant from Freud's idea of the drives. There appear to be “prewired” innate patterns in the infant for responsiveness to the environment and to the mother from the beginning. If this is so, there must be comparable “prewiring” in the mother (or other primary caregivers) which readies her to respond to the baby. Thus we are confronted with a new biology of the interpersonal realm, which, surprisingly for the interpersonalists, returns us to a point not far from where the debate between the intrapsychic and interpersonal realms began.

How Useful is the Borderline Concept?

Gerald Adler MD

Gerald Adler

West End House
16 Blossom Street
Boston, MA 02114

Gerald Adler  

Psychoanalytic theory is most useful when it is clearly based upon clinical observations and can help the analyst or therapist both to understand the patient and to intervene clinically in ways helpful to that patient and to similar ones. Yet we all know that different clinicians can make careful observations of their patients and arrive at significantly different formulations about the theoretical and clinical issues that explain their patients' behavior and intrapsychic structures.

We realize that the data a patient presents to us are influenced by a number of factors (Adler, 1986). In addition to the personality characteristics of the patient and his or her problems, the setting as well as the personal and interpersonal qualities of the data collector are important. Is the patient talking to a researcher, therapist, or analyst? Is he in a short-term or initial-treatment setting, or in an ongoing psychotherapy or psychoanalysis? What are the clinician's actual personality characteristics, and how do these qualities interact with the specific patient, and therefore play a role in the patient's responses?

Dr. Adler is Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Society & Institute; he is also Director of Medical Student Education in Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital.

W. Meissner S.J.

W. Meissner

129 Mount Auburn Street
Cambridge, MA 02138

W. Meissner  

The purpose of the present study is to evaluate the contribution of the Kris Study Group to the understanding of borderline psychopathology and to try to place that contribution in perspective. I approach this task by way of contrasting the Kris group findings and the contributions of Otto Kernberg. In large measure, the report of the Kris Study Group (Abend et al., 1983) is structured along the lines of a continuing dialogue with Kernberg. In tracing the contrast between these two approaches, I aim at subsuming them under a broader perspective, namely, one provided by the borderline spectrum (Meissner, 1984a). I argue that both Kernberg and the Kris group are looking at and working with patients who represent different ranges within the borderline spectrum, so that their respective observations, descriptions, theoretical formulations, and forms of technical intervention are dictated more by the nature of the underlying pathology than by any verifiable theoretical differences.

It should be noted that even their view of borderline pathology differs. The Kris group tends to regard borderline character structure as relatively stable, tending neither to become markedly psychotic nor to improve very much. They were more likely to see impediments as varying along a quantitative continuum of different degrees of severity (Buie, 1985)

Dr. Meissner is Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute; University Professor of Psychoanalysis, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA.

It has been ten years since the Kris Study Group of the New York Psychoanalytic Institute completed its study of borderline pathology, and perhaps seven years since we finished our work on the manuscript of Borderline. Since then, much new material on the subject has appeared, including a number of contributions by other analysts, some of whose views are represented in this publication, in addition to a number of published reviews of our book. We three have also, singly and in combination, participated in a number of discussions and panels devoted to the topic. We have continued to discuss this subject among ourselves and with interested colleagues, to review the recent literature, and to treat borderline patients in our offices.

This activity underlines the high level of interest the borderline problem holds for all of us concerned with their treatment, and testifies to the lively intellectual ferment and scientific curiosity that characterizes our present state of knowledge. Stendhal as a Replacement Child: The Theme of the Dead Child in Stendhal's Writings

Emmett Wilson MD

Emmett Wilson

Canal Road, R.D. 1 Box 262
Princeton, N.J. 08540

Emmett Wilson  

The french novelist henri beyle (1783-1842), best known under his pseudonym, Stendhal, used the child as a recurring theme in his work. Though his novels are curiously lacking in direct depiction of children or childhood, we find instead themes of pregnancy, the child as yet unborn, childbirth, the child in danger, and the child that has died. Previous Stendhal scholars and critics have noted the presence of this theme in Stendhal's writings, but as yet neither the psychological background nor the explanation for this curious focus on the dead or endangered child have been elaborated. In this paper I suggest certain aspects of Stendhal's own childhood developmental history that will help us understand his strange fascination with the themes of death and childbirth.

Among the examples that illustrate this theme in Stendhal is the agonized scene in The Red and the Black between its hero, Julien, and Mme de Rênal, concerning the illness and possible death of the latter's young son. Mme de Rênal, unbalanced by her anguish and worry over her son's illness, is ready to confess to her husband the affair with Julien in the hope that Heaven will pardon her guilty love and save the child's life.

Emmett Wilson, Jr. is in the private practice of child psychiatry in Princeton, NJ.

Sander Abend MD

Sander Abend

1040 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10028

Sander Abend  

I do not want you to think that I plan to avoid the question this conference asks us to consider, but I must tell you at the outset that I think you have directed attention to the wrong dilemma. Freud was reputed to have said that history would remember him for discovering that children have sexual lives and dreams have meaning; however, both discoveries were already familiar to every nursemaid in Vienna. Although the implications of Freud's findings about dreams are not in question here today, the same cannot be said about his views of the consequences of children's sexual lives. The evolution of psychoanalytic thought is filled with divergences labeled as advances by their proponents and as avoidances or mistakes by their critics. At the heart of the vast majority of those differences is one or another variation on the question of whether or not infantile sexuality is as important in the mental lives of human beings as Freud said it was. Is the dynamic unconscious as much a repository of fantasies embodying childrens' sexual wishes, worries, and theories as Freud believed, or do other desires, issues, and concerns occupy a more important place in development and adult character and behavior than Freud realized?

Case Discussion and Position Statement

Ernest Wolf MD

Ernest Wolf

1333 Tower Road
Winnetka, IL 60093

Ernest Wolf  

The unresolved dilemma of defining an interpersonal or an intrapsychic dimension in psychoanalysis is in essence a task of defining the outlines of the field in which we make our scientific observations. For unless we define our field and decide what are data and what are not, we cannot make any useful observations at all. Our dilemma arises from the uncontested fact that the two dimensions are intertwined: intrapsychic events are powerfully influenced by extrapsychic ones, especially the interpersonal dimension, and vice versa: the extrapsychic sphere is the arena in which the individual acts out his intrapsychic dynamics. Though it is possible conceptually to separate these two dimensions, one can try to describe only intrapsychically or only interpersonally. In self psychology we have chosen not to separate these two dimensions that far. We talk about selfobject experiences which are intrapsychic happenings that are closely linked to extrapsychic events. I say “linked” because I want to avoid saying “caused.” For example, when a child stumbles, and falling on its face, gets all shaken up, momentarily confused, and disoriented, it may need help to quickly be put together again. An appropriately attuned mother will pick up the child, hold it close, and let her child absorb her calmness.

Dr. Wolf is Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis and Assistent Professor of Psychiatry, Northwestern University Medical School.

The charge to prepare a position statement on “The Therapeutic Dimension” is based on several assumptions. First, of course, is that one has a position that can be articulated; second, that it is distinctive enough to stand comparison with another's stated position. A third necessity is that one have some case material about which one can take a stand to define one's position.

We have been supplied with case material in which are condensed some aspects of a patient's personal, family, and therapeutic histories. Most of the account of the sessions is couched at a level so far from the actual phenomena of the analytic situation that in scale it resembles an aerial photograph rather than the portrait I would like to have. Events, or rather tendencies, in the patient's life and analysis are described in the language of generalized psychosexual conflict and in such a way that it would be difficult to distinguish this patient and her analysis from any other.

The psychoanalytic study of the developmental significance of sibling relationships has suffered from a contempt of familiarity. The imminence of personal, familial, organizational, and clinical associations to the topic make it difficult to reflect upon it spontaneously with sufficient detachment (Segal, 1957). The impingement on our professional working selves of our own or others' sibling behaviors in our homes, clinics, psychoanalytic societies, or wider professional communities has left the familiarity and the vastness of the topic caught in defensive collusion between experience and theory. This has resulted in an overly exclusive emphasis on the effects of the primary relationship with the parents and the tendency to relegate the sibling to a “real object” model only.
